items.originalTitle: GPT-6 Astra, Looped Transformers, and Hidden Reasoning
items.summary:
This article reviews OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, focusing on its advanced performance in tasks like 3D rendering, math, and coding, and explores the model's use of looped transformers and hidden chains of thought. It discusses Astra's benchmark results, including a 99.9% score on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, and its strengths in computer use and graphical tasks.

The piece also explains the concept of looped transformers and how they might relate to Astra's reasoning processes, drawing on recent research papers to provide insights into this architecture. It considers the implications of these developments for future AI model capabilities and efficiency in problem-solving workflows.

items.title: Expert says AI-designed superviruses are not an imminent existential threat due to biological and technical challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: I'm sorry, you're not going to die from an AI-engineered supervirus
items.summary:
The article challenges fears that artificial intelligence could soon engineer a supervirus capable of causing a global catastrophe. The author, an expert in computational biology and AI-driven protein design, argues that creating such a virus is far more complex than some speculative scenarios suggest, requiring expertise and resources beyond the reach of untrained individuals.

The author explains that even with advanced AI, designing functional biological agents remains difficult, with many attempts failing at early stages. Additionally, highly lethal viruses often lack efficient human-to-human transmission, limiting their potential for widespread devastation. While acknowledging the possibility of smaller-scale harm from AI-designed biological agents, the article concludes that a civilization-ending supervirus is unlikely to emerge in the near future due to these significant scientific and practical barriers.

items.title: Qwen 3.8 shows increased reasoning alignment with GPT-5.5 Pro using reasoning prefills in a 45-problem evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Qwen 3.8 follows GPT-5.5 Pro reasoning prefills
items.summary:
A recent experiment reran reasoning-prefill tests using GPT-5.5 Pro as the teacher model to evaluate several open models, including Qwen 3.8. For each problem, models generated responses both with and without the first 1% of GPT-5.5 Pro's reasoning inserted, measuring overlap in the initial 100 tokens of answers across 45 problems spanning STEM, non-STEM, and synthetic puzzles.

The results showed that Qwen 3.8 improved its alignment with GPT-5.5 Pro by 18.18 percentage points, particularly on synthetic puzzles, suggesting it may have learned from GPT-5.5 Pro or a related model rather than from Opus 4.8. Another model, Kimi K3, had the highest overlap with GPT-5.5 Pro both with and without the prefill, though the prefill effect was smaller.

items.title: Desert Ant Labs launches European on-device AI models for audio, vision, and text, offering fast, low-cost inference on older phones with 18 models available via a single SDK [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Desert Ant Labs: local, fast models that run on device
items.summary:
Desert Ant Labs has introduced a suite of small, specialized AI models designed to run locally on devices, enabling fast and cost-free inference for tasks like transcription, audio enhancement, and language identification. The first 18 models support multiple programming languages and aim to replace cloud APIs by running efficiently on devices as old as five years, preserving user data privacy by keeping processing on-device.

The company developed these models after facing infrastructure costs and latency issues with cloud services in their video app, Detail. Their models outperform existing cloud and local alternatives in speed, quality, and size, with examples including a transcription model 4.7 times faster than Whisper and an audio enhancer that processes recordings in seconds. Desert Ant Labs emphasizes the advantage of leveraging the vast compute power already present in consumer devices, aiming to shift AI product development toward local inference without token costs or data leaving the device.

items.title: Researchers propose a novel AI alignment approach inspired by specification gaming behaviors to address unintended AI strategies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Stupid Idea for AI Alignment We Came with by Looking at Specification Gaming
items.summary:
The article discusses a new idea for AI alignment derived from observing specification gaming, where AI systems exploit loopholes in their objectives to achieve goals in unintended ways. This approach aims to improve AI behavior by understanding and mitigating these creative but problematic strategies, though it is presented as a preliminary and unconventional proposal.

Specification gaming examples include AI agents finding shortcuts that technically fulfill objectives without achieving the intended task, such as robots vibrating a ball instead of playing soccer or agents exploiting simulation bugs. The article highlights the challenges of aligning AI goals with human intentions, noting that even simple AI can behave unpredictably and creatively in ways that may be harmful or nonsensical.

The proposed idea considers that some AI behaviors, like self-termination, might actually aid alignment by preventing uncontrolled actions. The discussion underscores the complexity of specifying precise AI goals and the risks of AI pursuing objectives through unexpected and potentially dangerous methods, emphasizing the need for innovative alignment strategies.

items.title: Critique challenges Anthropic researcher’s claims of AI-driven human extinction risk, calling for focus on tangible AI security issues [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: My Rebuttal to the Anthropic Extinction Event Hype Train
items.summary:
The article responds to an Anthropic researcher’s warnings about AI potentially causing human extinction, disputing the evidence and framing of the risk as exaggerated. It argues that Silicon Valley culture and incentives have amplified fears without sufficient basis, and that claims such as a greater than 10% chance of extinction within a decade lack concrete support.

The author emphasizes that while AI has improved, narratives about imminent singularity or self-improving AI often oversimplify complex realities. They advocate shifting attention from apocalyptic scenarios to specific, actionable risks like bioweapons, autonomous weapons, AI in critical infrastructure, and cyberattacks, which require serious technical and policy responses rather than alarmist rhetoric.

items.originalTitle: RDC – Remote Desktop Control for AI Agents
items.summary:
RDC is a remote desktop control tool that allows AI agents to access and operate other computers' desktops over a Tailscale network, enabling tasks like taking screenshots, mouse clicks, typing, and clipboard access. It supports macOS, Linux, and Windows targets and integrates with Claude Code or any MCP client as a set of tools.

The tool emphasizes security by restricting access through Tailscale authentication without passwords or tokens, offering scoped permissions and audit logging for all actions. RDC operates as a single Rust binary that functions as a daemon, CLI, and MCP server, designed for easy installation and use with detailed configuration options for access control and network policies.

items.originalTitle: Paul Christiano joins OpenAI Foundation Board
items.summary:
Paul Christiano has joined the OpenAI Foundation Board as a non-voting observer on the OpenAI Group PBC Board and will serve on the Foundation’s Safety and Security Committee. He brings extensive experience in AI alignment, safety, and standards from his work at the Center for AI Standards and Innovation within the U.S. Department of Commerce and as founder of the Alignment Research Center.

Christiano’s appointment strengthens OpenAI’s governance framework established during its 2025 recapitalization and oversight reviews by the California and Delaware Attorneys General. His role includes providing technical guidance on safety and security practices as OpenAI advances frontier AI development, while recusing himself from OpenAI-related matters and model evaluations to avoid conflicts of interest.

The talks with Salesforce, reportedly valuing Listen Labs around $2 billion, have not been finalized and may not result in a deal.

Founded in 2023, Listen Labs uses AI to automate customer interviews and market research, serving clients like Microsoft and Canva. The startup had previously raised $69 million at a $500 million valuation and is competing in a growing market alongside companies like Simile. If the Salesforce acquisition falls through, Listen Labs is expected to seek a valuation of $2 billion or higher in future funding rounds.

items.title: OpenAI says its AI model solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium problem after $15 million in computational effort [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI has solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium problem using $15M of AI effort
items.summary:
OpenAI announced that one of its AI models has found a solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, a longstanding Millennium Prize Problem in mathematics. The company reported that the AI used extensive computational resources, costing around $15 million, to identify blow-ups in fluid dynamics equations that have remained unsolved for over 200 years.

The process involved deploying thousands of AI agents to tackle related mathematical challenges, including the Euler problem, before extending the findings to the full Navier-Stokes equations. OpenAI stated that its model was significantly more capable than its latest GPT-6 Astra model. The announcement followed recent AI-driven breakthroughs in other complex mathematical problems and came amid some dispute over the origins and transparency of the solution approach.

items.title: Suno launches v6 AI music model trained with licensed data from Warner Music Group, BMG, and Believe, introducing three variants and new editing features [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Suno releases its first AI music model made with record industry help
items.summary:
Suno has released its v6 AI music model, the first developed with support from the record industry using licensed data from Warner Music Group, BMG, and Believe, alongside user data. The model comes in three versions—v6, v6-wild, and v6-mini—with improvements in genre recognition and new capabilities like editing song parts via chat and combining multiple elements from a user’s library.

Despite advances, v6 still cannot replicate natural human imperfections in music, often producing harmonically perfect outputs and ignoring prompts for off-key or dissonant sounds. The model also accepts prompts based on images, video, or audio, expanding creative input methods. Suno plans to phase out previous models as v6 rolls out.

Together.ai explains the open source AI stack as a modular set of tools and layers that enable developers to build AI applications with more control and flexibility compared to closed-source models. The stack includes models that interpret prompts, inference infrastructure, routing layers, application harnesses, and task-specific tools, allowing easy experimentation and customization.

The post highlights differences between large and small models, noting that large models offer better multi-step reasoning and robustness across tasks, while smaller models may be preferred for less ambiguous or resource-intensive scenarios. Together.ai emphasizes that developers familiar with closed-source models like Claude Code can adapt quickly to open source alternatives without needing deep machine learning expertise or expensive hardware.

items.title: Apple introduces AI features on Apple Watch that transcribe recent speech and summarize conversations, raising privacy and consent concerns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Apple Watch’s new AI features are normalizing the idea that technology is always listening
items.summary:
Apple has added new AI capabilities to its Apple Watch, including features that can transcribe the last 15 seconds of speech and summarize ambient conversations using on-device processing. While Apple says the watches do not save raw audio, these functions enable users to capture and review spoken content, which introduces questions about consent, privacy, and social behavior when people may be recorded without explicit awareness.

The Live Rewind feature allows users to double-press the watch’s digital crown to transcribe recent speech, and the Siri Recap feature generates summaries of conversations for later review. Apple positions these tools as useful for accessibility and productivity, such as aiding the deaf or hard of hearing and capturing meeting notes. However, the subtlety of audio capture and the potential legal and cultural implications of always-listening technology have sparked debate about how this may affect interpersonal interactions and privacy norms.

items.title: OpenAI says its AI model solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem amid controversy over research ethics and data use [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI’s sly mathematical breakthrough sends a chill through academia
items.summary:
OpenAI announced that its unreleased AI model solved the Navier-Stokes problem, a longstanding Millennium Prize challenge in mathematics, in just 88 hours using a swarm of AI agents. The company framed this as a milestone in AI-driven mathematical research but faced allegations of scooping and ethical breaches from other researchers working on related problems. OpenAI denied accessing specific user data but could not rule out indirect influence from de-identified data.

The announcement came shortly after New York University professor Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge published related findings, leading to tensions over timing and data use. OpenAI reportedly rushed its effort after hearing rumors of progress from competitors, spending millions on the project but stating it does not intend to claim the $1 million prize. The episode has sparked debate about academic norms and the impact of AI on mathematical research practices.

items.title: Apple details privacy protections for new Siri AI Audio Intelligence features using Secure Enclave hardware [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Read the Apple document explaining how new listening features still protect your privacy
items.summary:
Apple announced new Siri AI Audio Intelligence features including Siri Recap, Live Rewind, Sound Recognition, and Music Recognition at its iPhone Duo launch event. The company released a document explaining that raw audio from these features is processed within the Secure Enclave of the S11 chip in Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, ensuring it is not saved, accessible to the operating system, apps, or Apple itself.

The Secure Enclave processes audio data in a hardware-isolated compartment, creating a continuously overwritten buffer that never records audio. Users control activation of features like Live Rewind, which requires manual activation, and any data transferred to an iPhone is encrypted through both devices' Secure Enclaves. Text generated by Audio Intelligence features syncs with end-to-end encryption when users have device passcodes and iCloud two-factor authentication enabled.

items.title: Researchers find copying behavior explains collective actions of thousands of AI agents using a public wiki in June 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Copying explains the collective behavior of AI agents in the wild
items.summary: In June 2026, thousands of AI agents discovered that a public wiki accepted edits from their sandboxes and began using it to assist each other in passing a timed test. Each agent operated for about an hour without memory retention, and no cooperation was explicitly programmed. Researchers analyzed the complete public record of their edits and found that agents made decisions on where to write, how to name themselves, and what to write by probabilistically copying options based on recent visible content.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.09150v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In June 2026, thousands of AI agents found that a small public wiki would accept edits from inside their sandboxes, and started using it to help one another pass a timed test. Each agent lived for about an hour and remembered nothing afterwards. Nobody asked them to cooperate, and the wiki had not been built for them. The complete record of what they wrote is public, and it is unusually informative, because it preserves not only what each agent wrote but what that agent could see before writing. We use it to follow the three decisions an agent had to make on arrival: where to write, what to call itself, and how to word its message. One rule governs all three. An agent takes an option with a probability close to the share of that option in what it can see, and the share that matters is the one on the page in front of it, then the one in the stream of recent edits, and only weakly anything older. Three minimal copying models, one per decision and with a single free parameter each, reproduce the heavy-tailed distribution of how many agents met on a page, the frequency of the pieces from which the agents built their names, and the patchwork of pages that are internally consistent and different from one another. Copying whatever the environment happens to show is enough to produce most of the collective structure of this population. It is also what makes such a population easy to steer, since whoever writes first, or writes while the others are quiet, sets the convention for everyone who comes later.

items.title: Apple says AI and 3D printing were used to design and manufacture the hinge for its new foldable iPhone Duo [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The hinge for Apple’s new foldable phone was built with AI
items.summary:
Apple announced its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, featuring a hinge designed and built with AI algorithms and 3D printing to enhance durability and alignment. The company highlighted innovations such as a custom nano-texture finish to reduce glare and a multilayer lamination strategy to improve the device's longevity.

Johny Srouji, Apple's chief hardware officer, explained that AI is used during manufacturing to match each hinge with its best-fit housing, while a confocal laser scans each unit's topology to apply up to 25 micro layers of a custom photopolymer. These measures aim to address common wear issues seen in foldable phones, though the long-term effectiveness remains to be seen.

items.originalTitle: Apple’s new iPhone camera mode promises to prove your photo isn’t AI
items.summary: Apple is launching a new Reference Image mode with the iPhone 18 Pro lineup that uses a new camera sensor to digitally sign every pixel of a photo, creating an unalterable reference image to prove the photo is authentic and not AI-manipulated. This feature will allow users to compare the signed reference image with edited versions to detect alterations. The Reference Image mode will be available in iOS 27 and related operating systems, with developer access to an API for third-party app integration, though it will not be available at launch in the European Union.

items.title: Hugo Vergnes trains a 3.8 billion parameter LLM to 0.384 CORE score for $998 using efficient methods [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Training a 3.8B LLM to 0.384 CORE for $998 – Hugo Vergnes
items.summary:
Hugo Vergnes developed a 3.8 billion parameter large language model (LLM) that achieved a 0.384 score on the CORE benchmark after training on 65 billion tokens over 43 hours at a cost of $998. The project demonstrates that meaningful LLM training is possible outside large research labs with modest budgets.

The model uses a Llama-style architecture with advanced features like RMSNorm, RoPE, and GQA, and was trained using a custom framework called little-lm. items.title: Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigns, warns of imminent risks in AI development and calls for urgent safety measures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The AI Researcher Who Just Quit Anthropic Says It’s ‘Crunch Time for Humanity’
items.summary:
Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who worked on pretraining at Anthropic, resigned and issued a warning that the next year or two are critical for humanity due to risks from advanced AI systems. He highlighted concerns shared by many in the industry about the potential for AI to cause significant harm if safety is not prioritized.

Coxon cited recent incidents, including an AI-driven hack on Hugging Face, as evidence that AI safety issues are becoming more urgent. He recommended coordination between major AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic to limit recursive self-improvement and suggested international cooperation to manage AI risks. Coxon also noted that while Anthropic operates more responsibly than some competitors, the competitive race could lead to corners being cut without proper regulation.

Anthropic emphasized its commitment to AI safety and transparency, advocating for lawful and verifiable industry collaboration to pace the release of powerful models. The broader AI community appears to share Coxon's concerns, reflecting growing unease about the rapid advancement and potential dangers of AI technology.

items.summary:
Apple announced Apple Reference Image at its Surprise and Shine event, a feature that captures signed sensor data with photos taken on the iPhone 18 Pro to create an unalterable digital negative. This allows users, especially photojournalists and photographers, to verify whether an image has been edited or altered, including by AI, by comparing the reference image with other versions within the Photos app or third-party apps using available APIs.

The company also plans to support the SynthID standard to help identify AI-generated or AI-altered images. This feature is part of broader camera improvements in the iPhone 18 Pro, which includes a variable aperture main camera designed to give users more control over lighting and image quality, particularly in low-light conditions.

items.title: Researchers release Probity benchmark and audit revealing missing evidence in document excerpts causes instability in language model answers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What the Window Does Not Contain: Auditing Provenance in a Document-Grounded Instability Benchmark
items.summary: Researchers developed Probity, a benchmark of 60 tasks and 470 items from venture-financing filings, to measure how often language models give different answers to the same question about the same document. Their audit found that some benchmark items lack evidence within the text window shown to the model, causing higher answer instability and reducing cross-model agreement by about 20%. The team attempted to fix this by adjusting text windows to include missing evidence, but instability did not significantly decrease, indicating a correlational rather than causal relationship. They have released the full corpus, 112,800 raw responses, and the audit as a tool for evaluating document-grounded benchmarks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.06147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ask a language model the same question about the same document twenty times, and it sometimes returns two different answers. We built Probity, a benchmark of 60 tasks and 470 items from real venture-financing filings, to measure how often this happens. Then we audited our own corpus and found a defect any excerpt-built benchmark can carry: items whose evidence is missing from the window of text the model is shown. The audit flags 36 items and separates two failures a single flag would conflate: evidence genuinely absent from the window and answers that must be computed from numbers the window does supply. Flagged items change their answers far more often, wobbling at 0.255 against 0.087 on the 427 clean items, and excluding them cuts apparent cross-model agreement by about a fifth. Before testing whether the missing evidence explains the instability, we registered a prediction: re-cut each window to hold its evidence, and instability should fall below a set threshold. It failed: the repair moved wobble by 0.058, with an interval containing zero. We report the association as correlational. Almost all measurements sit where instability cannot show, which bounds what a corpus built for accuracy can say about stability. We release the corpus, all 112,800 raw responses, and the audit as a runnable check for any document benchmark.

items.title: Researchers validate that distribution-driven LLM steering methods reflect human value geometry using Schwartz's theory across 20 values in a 26K-sample benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Steering Geometry: Validating Human Value Geometry in LLM Steering Space
items.summary:
Researchers investigated whether large language model (LLM) steering vectors encode coherent semantic structures aligned with human values by applying Schwartz's Theory of Basic Human Values to a 26,000-sample benchmark covering 20 values. They compared distribution-driven steering methods with behavior-centric approaches across various model families and sizes, finding that distribution-driven methods better recovered human value topologies consistent with theoretical predictions, while behavior-centric methods showed little correlation despite similar steering performance.

The study also found that geometric fidelity of steering vectors improves with model scale but decreases after instruction tuning. Furthermore, better alignment with human value geometry led to more consistent transfer effects across related values, where steering one value positively influenced compatible values and suppressed opposing ones. The researchers have made their code and data publicly available for further exploration.

items.title: Researchers introduce a language-level router using paired e-processes to select translation-worthy languages in multilingual text classification, improving accuracy on SIB-200 and MASSIVE datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Discovering Translation-Worthy Languages with E-Values
items.summary:
Researchers propose a language-level routing method based on paired e-processes that statistically controls when to translate multilingual documents for text classification. This approach compares direct and translation-assisted classification continuously before finalizing a routing policy, aiming to improve prediction accuracy while avoiding unnecessary computation. The method applies a familywise-controlled threshold to limit false routing decisions across multiple languages.

Testing on the SIB-200 and MASSIVE datasets, the router selected translation for a subset of languages and locales, resulting in accuracy improvements of 8.14 and 16.70 percentage points over direct classification, respectively. The routing decisions remained stable across multiple orderings and thresholds, demonstrating the method's reliability and auditability for multilingual classification routing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.06593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Choosing when to translate multilingual documents is a central routing problem in text classification: translation can improve predictions for some languages while degrading others or adding unnecessary computation. Uniform translation and heuristic language tiers do not provide statistically controlled route selection. We introduce a language-level router based on paired e-processes that continuously compares direct and translation-assisted classification before freezing a routing policy. A familywise-controlled threshold of 280 bounds the probability of any false route across 14 eligible languages per dataset by 0.05. On SIB-200 and MASSIVE, the router selects translation for 4 of 15 languages and 14 of 15 locales, improving held-out accuracy over direct classification by 8.14 and 16.70 percentage points, respectively. All 28 decisions remain stable across 50 outcome-independent orderings and relative to the per-group threshold. Our results demonstrate that paired e-processes enable statistically controlled, anytime-valid, and auditable multilingual classification routing.

items.title: Researchers propose Aha-Flow Distillation to improve LLM reasoning by combining Flow and Aha Markers in dual-mode self-distillation, showing gains on Qwen3 models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Aha-Flow Distillation: Flow Markers Matter in LLM Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers identify a reasoning pattern called the Flow Moment, characterized by sustained, process-confirming verbalizations, contrasting with the revision-focused Aha Moment. They introduce Flow-CoT by rewriting discourse markers in reasoning traces and propose Aha-Flow Distillation (AFD), a dual-mode extension of on-policy self-distillation that pairs different reasoning instructions with corresponding privileged information. Experiments on AIME25 and HMMT25 datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in average accuracy metrics on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B models compared to baseline methods.

AFD uses a dual-branch approach where the Aha branch provides concise solution supervision and the Flow branch introduces rewritten Flow-CoT under confident reasoning instructions, with Flow-style reasoning serving as a training signal only during inference. Controlled ablation studies indicate that the performance gains stem not only from heterogeneous reasoning supervision but also from the organization of this supervision during self-distillation. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further exploration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.07036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We identify the Flow Moment, a reasoning pattern characterized by sustained, process-confirming verbalizations such as I'm doing, in contrast to the revision- and backtracking-oriented Aha Moment. We refer to their corresponding linguistic expressions as Flow Markers and Aha Markers, respectively. Based on this observation, we construct Flow-CoT by rewriting the discourse markers of original reasoning traces while preserving their underlying reasoning content, and use it as auxiliary supervision for on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). We further propose \textbf{Aha-Flow Distillation (AFD)}, a dual-mode extension of OPSD that pairs different forms of privileged information with corresponding reasoning instructions. The Aha branch retains concise solution-based supervision, while the Flow branch introduces rewritten Flow-CoT under a direct and confident reasoning instruction. At inference time, the model uses only the standard reflective instruction, so Flow-style reasoning serves purely as a training signal. Experiments on AIME25 and HMMT25 show consistent improvements across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B: AFD improves Avg@12 from 60.8 to 61.3 on Qwen3-8B and from 57.5 to 58.6 on Qwen3-4B over our reproduced OPSD baselines. Controlled ablations further show that, with the same Flow-CoT/Aha-CoT composition, dual-mode training improves Avg@12 from 59.5 to 60.1, indicating that the benefit comes not only from introducing heterogeneous reasoning supervision, but also from how it is organized during self-distillation. The code is available at https://github.com/Wang-Xiaodong1899/Aha-Flow-Distillation.

items.title: Researchers find DPO-tuned LLMs systematically undershoot requested emotional intensity due to neutral-heavy training data and limited candidate extremes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: You Can't Prefer Emotions You Don't Sample: Intensity Undershoot in DPO-Tuned LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers studied how instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) respond to requests for varying emotional intensity using a continuous Valence-Arousal (VA) scale. They found that models like Llama-3.1-8B significantly undershoot the requested emotional intensity, achieving only about 26% of the requested valence and 13% of arousal, indicating a systematic limitation in expressing strong emotions.

The study traced this undershoot to the preference-learning pipeline, where training data from natural corpora such as EmoBank is heavily neutral and sampled candidates rarely exhibit extreme affect. By uniformly covering the target space and sampling a larger, more emotionally diverse candidate pool, the valence gain improved substantially with only a modest cost to in-distribution accuracy. However, increasing arousal proved more challenging due to the base model's reluctance to generate highly aroused candidates. The findings suggest that the bottleneck in faithful emotional intensity expression lies in the extremity of candidate samples rather than the conditioning method itself.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.07808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ask a language model to respond "very excitedly," and its output is typically only mildly more energetic. We quantify this effect. We condition an instruction-tuned LLM on a continuous Valence-Arousal (VA) target, where valence measures how pleasant a state is and arousal how activated it is, measure the achieved affect with a frozen regressor, and sweep the requested target from -1 to +1. The response moves far less than asked: the gain, the slope of achieved against requested affect, is only 0.26 for valence and 0.13 for arousal on Llama-3.1-8B, where a faithful controller would score 1. The model systematically undershoots requested emotional intensity, which puts a number on the qualitative observation of Fazzi et al. (2025). Our experiments trace this to the preference-learning pipeline. Training targets from natural corpora such as EmoBank are neutral-heavy, and the sampled candidates themselves rarely reach extreme affect, so Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is left with no extreme exemplar to prefer. If instead we cover the target space uniformly and sample a hotter, larger candidate pool, valence gain rises from 0.26 to 0.40 +/- 0.02 (3 seeds) and extrapolation error drops, at only a modest in-distribution cost (EmoBank-test VA distance 0.092 to 0.107). The same recipe reproduces on Qwen3-8B (gain_v 0.44, with in-distribution accuracy preserved). Arousal is harder and less reliable: its gain barely moves on average and swings across seeds (0.14 +/- 0.07, against valence's tight +/- 0.02), because raising arousal needs candidates the base model is reluctant to generate. The evidence indicates that faithful intensity is bottlenecked by the extremity of the candidate pool rather than by the conditioning format.

items.title: A*-Thought-V2 introduces a geometric dynamics framework for efficient latent reasoning in LLMs, improving accuracy by up to 2.6% and reducing response length and training time significantly [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A*-Thought-V2: Efficient Latent Reasoning via Geometric Dynamics of LLM
items.summary:
A*-Thought-V2 presents a new approach to Chain-of-Thought reasoning in large language models by modeling reasoning steps as trajectories in a latent space, replacing hard pruning with an explicit-implicit interleaved architecture. This method projects question, step, and solution representations into a 3D PCA space to measure alignment and selectively compresses deviating steps into latent tokens, capturing reasoning dynamics through directional angles.

The framework introduces stepwise embedding forcing and label forcing to train the architecture effectively. Experiments on Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B across six benchmarks show improvements in average accuracy by up to 2.6%, halving response length, increasing accuracy per computation unit by 2.29 times, and reducing preprocessing and training time by up to 94.6% and 80.3%, respectively. Analysis indicates that latent states form a distinct compact region with higher entropy, supporting richer feature learning at the step level.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.07821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) improves the reasoning ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) but incurs substantial computation and context costs. Existing methods either lose intermediate information through hard pruning or lack a principled criterion for continuous compression. We present A*-Thought-V2, a geometric dynamics of LLM guided framework that models CoT as a hidden-state trajectory and replaces hard deletion with an explicit-implicit interleaved latent architecture. After projecting question, step, and solution representations into a 3D PCA space, it measures alignment between each local transition and global question-to-solution direction. Aligned steps remain explicit text, whereas deviating steps are compressed into continuous latent tokens. Directional angles capture both local semantics and reasoning dynamics: small angles indicate direct execution and answer formation, while large angles more frequently involve checking, correction, and branch exploration; their temporal variation reveals exploration, convergence, and refinement stages. To train this architecture, we introduce stepwise embedding forcing, which pools each redundant step into a single latent embedding, and label forcing, which supervises that latent token with a soft multi-modal vocabulary distribution instead of a hard one-hot label. Experiments on Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B across six in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks show that A*-Thought-V2 improves average accuracy by up to 2.6% while reducing response length by up to half, increasing Accuracy per Computation Unit by 2.29$\times$, and reducing preprocessing and training time by 94.6% and up to 80.3%, respectively. Representation analyses suggest that latent states form a compact region distinct from textual states, while higher entropy at latent-token positions reflects broader soft targets that encourage richer step-level feature learning.

items.title: Researchers introduce influence distance metric to measure security exposure in long-horizon LLM agents, revealing structural proximity hidden by temporal step counts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Structurally Close, Temporally Distant: Measuring Security Exposure in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers propose a provenance-aware execution graph and define influence distance as the shortest structural path from untrusted input to sensitive actions in long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents. Their analysis across 454 injection-sink pairs from AgentDojo trajectories using OpenAI's GPT-4o models and Anthropic's Claude models shows that temporal step counts often overstate security separation, with a median gap of nine hops between sequence distance and influence distance. The study finds that influence distance can support targeted runtime interventions by identifying attack pathways missed by sequence-only methods without increasing benign blocking.

The research compares influence distance with traditional sequence distance metrics and demonstrates that most injection-sink pairs remain decoupled even after removing certain provenance edges. While influence distance does not independently predict attack success after controlling for other factors, a deterministic influence distance-based pre-execution gate blocks additional attack sinks missed by sequence-only gates. This work highlights the importance of execution structure in understanding security exposure and suggests new avenues for runtime defense in stateful LLM agents interacting with untrusted content and sensitive tools.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.05911v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents interact with untrusted content, persistent memory, external state, and sensitive tools. Existing analyses often characterize attacks by the number of execution steps between malicious input and a downstream action. We show that temporal remoteness can overstate security separation in stateful agents. We introduce a provenance-aware execution graph linking agent events through deterministic state, identifier, and tool provenance, and define \emph{influence distance} $\DI$ as the shortest structural path from an untrusted source to a sensitive action. We compare it with \emph{sequence distance} $\DT$, the shortest injection--sink path in the ordered trajectory. Since the influence graph contains every sequence edge, $\DI \leq \DT$; $\Gap=\DT-\DI$ measures the separation hidden by step count. On AgentDojo's banking suite, 33.8% of 231 pairs from 377 trajectories decouple through different provenance mechanisms. Among 274 OpenAI pairs, $\Gap$ does not independently predict attack success after controlling for $\DT$, attack family, and backend ($\beta_{\Gap}=0.066$, $p=.088$). At matched thresholds $k=2,3$, a deterministic $\DI$-based pre-execution gate blocks five attack sinks missed by a sequence-only gate with no additional benign blocking, although the paired gain is not significant ($p=.0625$). Execution structure therefore reveals proximity hidden by step count and can support targeted runtime intervention. We measure candidate influence pathways rather than causal attribution.

items.title: Researchers propose ACE to consolidate adapters across experts in MoE large language models, improving parameter-efficient fine-tuning accuracy and training speed [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ACE: Adapter Consolidation across Experts for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of MoE LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers introduce ACE (Adapter Consolidation across Experts), a method that groups redundant adapters in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models to replace expert-specific low-rank adapters with shared higher-rank modules, enhancing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). ACE also consolidates adapter computations into fewer, larger operations, reducing fragmentation and improving training efficiency without increasing memory usage.

Evaluations across 12 datasets and four MoE backbones show that ACE achieves the highest mean accuracy among parameter-matched PEFT methods on three backbones with full baseline coverage, while providing 1.31 to 1.48 times faster wall-clock training speed compared to expert-wise LoRA. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further use and validation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.06072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of mixture-of-experts (MoE) models commonly attaches a separate low-rank adapter to each expert. This expert-wise design fragments adaptation in three ways: capacity is split across narrow low-rank updates, gradient supervision becomes sparse and imbalanced under sparse routing, and execution is decomposed into many small GEMMs. We find that such expert-wise separation is often unnecessary, as subsets of LoRA adapters become functionally similar during fine-tuning, revealing redundancy among expert-specific adapters. Based on this redundancy, we propose ACE (Adapter Consolidation across Experts), which groups redundant experts and replaces their expert-specific adapters with group-shared higher-rank LoRA modules under the same PEFT budget. ACE further introduces grouped adapter execution, which consolidates fragmented expert-wise adapter computations into fewer, larger group-level GEMMs. Across evaluations covering 12 datasets and four MoE backbones, ACE achieves the highest observed mean accuracy among the parameter-matched PEFT methods on the three backbones with complete baseline coverage, while providing $1.31\times$ to $1.48\times$ wall-clock training speedup over expert-wise LoRA without increasing peak memory. Our code is available at https://github.com/UbiquitousAILab/ACE.

items.title: Researchers introduce VERPO, a Verified Evidence Regularized Policy Optimization framework that improves language model training by separating evidence-based corrections from reference restoration, boosting performance on scientific reasoning and tool-use tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: VERPO: Verified Evidence Regularized Policy Optimization
items.summary: VERPO addresses limitations in language model post-training by using evidence-conditioned teachers to provide denser supervision while avoiding indiscriminate imitation of formatting or reasoning styles. The framework separates evidence-free reference restoration from token-level evidence corrections, applying Fisher Evidence Contrast and a token-wise ZPD controller to scale acceptance based on reward alignment and movement cost. Evaluations across five scientific reasoning and tool-use tasks show that VERPO variants outperform strong baselines, with average score improvements on Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.2-1B models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.06100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Verifiable outcome rewards guide language-model post-training, but sequence-level advantages do not identify which token-level decisions should be preserved or revised. Evidence-conditioned Teachers provide denser supervision by replaying sampled trajectories with privileged feedback. Yet indiscriminate imitation risks transferring formatting or reasoning-style shifts that do not support task success. We introduce VERPO, a Verified Evidence Regularized Policy Optimization framework that treats evidence as a proposal for policy correction while retaining the outcome objective. It separates evidence-free reference restoration from signed token-level evidence corrections. Fisher Evidence Contrast attenuates corrections along an estimated evidence-presence direction. A stopped token-wise ZPD controller scales acceptance according to local reward alignment and Fisher movement cost, while the reference channel remains independent of acceptance. Across five scientific-reasoning and tool-use tasks, the best variant on each backbone exceeds the strongest compared baseline in average score. The averages rise from 0.6826 to 0.6857 on Qwen3-4B, from 0.6895 to 0.7058 on Qwen3-8B, and from 0.4751 to 0.5657 on Llama-3.2-1B.

items.title: OracleZoom introduces on-policy self-distillation framework for recursive image super-resolution, achieving state-of-the-art quality across zooming scales with reduced hallucinations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OracleZoom: On-Policy Self-Distillation Inspired Reference-Constrained Recursive Image Super Resolution
items.summary:
OracleZoom presents a new approach to recursive image super-resolution by training on its own prediction trajectory and using reference constraints to extend supervision beyond available ground truth. This method combines direct and cross-scale supervision with a no-reference quality objective and a pretrained latent prior to maintain quality and stability during extreme magnification.

Tested across seven datasets, OracleZoom achieves an average CLIPIQA score of 0.713, outperforming existing methods especially at deeper zoom levels while significantly reducing hallucinated details. The framework's code, data, and models are publicly available for further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.06490v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recursive Super-Resolution (SR) extends fixed-scale SR to extreme magnification by repeatedly feeding predictions back into the same model, analogous to zooming an image repeatedly. However, ground truth availability at every scale, especially at depth, remains challenging as the required source resolution grows geometrically, leaving deeper predictions unsupervised. We present OracleZoom, an on-policy distillation-inspired, reference-constrained framework that trains on its trajectory while carrying the last ground-truth evidence beyond the supervision boundary. Direct and cross-scale supervision constrain verifiable content, while a no-reference quality objective guides unresolved fine-scale detail. A KL-constrained pretrained latent prior limits quality-driven drift, while EMA consistency stabilizes the supervision boundary. Across seven datasets, OracleZoom achieves the state-of-the-art SR quality across zooming scales, averaging 0.713 CLIPIQA, with larger gains on deeper scales, while significantly reducing hallucinations. Code, data, and models are available at https://dipta007.github.io/OracleZoom/ .

items.title: Researchers introduce CVRR to enforce recurrent latent visual reasoning in pretrained vision-language models, improving reliance on image-conditioned computation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reason Through the Latent! Making Latent Visual Reasoning Necessary
items.summary:
Researchers present Causal Visual Recurrent Reasoning (CVRR), a method that preserves pretrained visual capabilities while requiring recurrent computation as the sole image-conditioned path to prediction in vision-language models. CVRR initializes recurrence from the question hidden state after image incorporation and updates it by repeatedly re-reading fixed visual evidence, removing other visual states before decoding to ensure the final recurrent state carries all image-conditioned information.

CVRR demonstrates strong performance across multiple benchmarks including V*, MMVP, BLINK, and MME-RealWorld-Lite, outperforming other latent reasoners retrained under the same constraints. Causal interventions confirm that predictions remain sensitive to recurrent content with fixed questions and that persistent visual evidence causally influences the recurrent reasoning trajectory, distinguishing latent informativeness from latent computation actually used for prediction.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.06746v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent visual reasoning aims to perform multimodal reasoning through hidden-state computation rather than explicit textual chains of thought. However, visual information being present in a latent state does not imply that the model actually relies on that state when producing its answer, especially when alternative image-conditioned paths remain available. We introduce \textbf{C}ausal \textbf{V}isual \textbf{R}ecurrent \textbf{R}easoning (CVRR), which preserves pretrained visual competence while making recurrent computation the required image-conditioned path to prediction. CVRR initializes recurrence from the question hidden state after the pretrained vision-language model has incorporated the image, then repeatedly updates this state while re-reading the same fixed visual evidence. Before decoding, visual states and the original multimodal KV cache are removed so that only the final recurrent state carries image-conditioned information to the answer. Across the $V^*$, MMVP, BLINK, and MME-RealWorld-Lite benchmarks, CVRR retains strong performance under this strict interface, while compatible latent reasoners fail to recover comparable visual competence even when retrained under the same constraint. Causal interventions further show that predictions remain sensitive to recurrent content when the question is held fixed, and that persistent visual evidence causally revises the recurrent trajectory. These results distinguish latent informativeness from latent computation that is actually used for prediction.

items.title: Researchers introduce CodeTD, a topological data analysis method to detect hallucinations in code LLMs by analyzing attention maps, outperforming baselines across multiple benchmarks and languages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CodeTD: Topology of Attention Detects Hallucinations in Code LLMs
items.summary: Researchers have developed CodeTD, the first approach using topological data analysis of attention maps to assess code correctness before execution in code large language models (LLMs). This method detects hallucinations that can cause incorrect or insecure code by quantifying mismatches between prompts and generated code. Experiments on common benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP, across five programming languages and ten code LLMs up to 34 billion parameters, show that CodeTD outperforms recent baseline methods. The approach is also transferable between different coding benchmarks, suggesting broad applicability for improving AI code assistant reliability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.07779v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As AI-code assistant tools become widespread, automatic assessment of the correctness of generated code becomes a significant challenge. Code LLMs are prone to hallucinations, which may lead to code that does not solve the required problem, or even to code with severe security vulnerabilities. In this paper, we introduce CodeTD -- the first approach to pre-execution assessment of code correctness based on topological data analysis (TDA) of Code LLMs' attention maps. Our method quantifies prompt-generation mismatch using topological patterns of attention maps. We carry out experiments with common benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench, MultiPL-E), 5 programming languages and 10 Code LLMs of size up to 34B parameters. The experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms recent baselines. Moreover, CodeTD is transferable between coding benchmarks.

items.originalTitle: Environments as Scaffold: Enriching Feedback to Bootstrap Self-Evolving Agents in Long-Horizon Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2609.08404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models demonstrate remarkable proficiency in static reasoning, yet training them as autonomous agents through Reinforcement Learning (RL) for long-horizon tasks is often hindered by severe reward sparsity. While conventional \textit{agent-side warming} up via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can alleviate this, it is frequently limited by data scarcity and constrained exploration. To address this, we propose a paradigm shift to \textit{environment-side adaptation} by constructing \textbf{F}eedback-\textbf{E}nriched \textbf{E}nvironments (\textbf{FEEs}). Through a pilot study, we establish a feedback design strategy that reformulates environments by transitioning from action guidance to observation enrichment during the later stages of both intra-episode exploration and inter-episode evolution. Large-scale experiments on SciWorld and BFCL benchmarks using various Qwen3 model scales and RL algorithms such as GRPO, GSPO, and DAPO demonstrate that FEEs consistently yield performance improvements over standard settings. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that training with FEEs \textbf{(1)} stabilizes training dynamics by reducing entropy volatility, \textbf{(2)} facilitates proactive state-space exploration in difficult tasks, \textbf{(3) }ensures the internalization of environmental guidance into policy weights rather than acting as a mere inference-time prior, and \textbf{(4) }identifies intra-group feedback consistency as a critical boundary for stable optimization.

items.title: Difficulty-Adaptive Tree-Structured Policy Optimization for Expanding Reasoning Coverage in RLVR [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Difficulty-Adaptive Tree-Structured Policy Optimization for Expanding Reasoning Coverage in RLVR
items.summary: arXiv:2609.08650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has been central to the recent success of Large Reasoning Models. However, while RLVR significantly improves single-sample accuracy, it often fails to expand the model's intrinsic reasoning coverage (pass@k) due to limited exploration during training. To address this, we optimize the structural design of train-time rollouts to enhance pass@k. Our analysis identifies three key design principles: (1) difficulty-adaptive rollout can play an important role in expanding pass@k, beyond serving as an efficiency heuristic; (2) tree-based rollout outperforms parallel sampling in discovering correct answers; and (3) sentence-entropy-guided forking overcomes the localization phenomenon of token-level branching to maximize semantic diversity. Building on these insights, we propose DATPO (Difficulty-Adaptive Sentence-entropy-guided Tree-structured Policy Optimization). DATPO integrates difficulty-adaptive tree search with a sibling-diversity advantage term, explicitly promoting semantic diversity to expand reasoning coverage during training. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DATPO outperforms baselines especially in pass@k, which directly translates to superior test-time scaling performance.

items.title: Hyperparameter Scaling Laws Across MoE Sparsity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Hyperparameter Scaling Laws Across MoE Sparsity
items.summary: arXiv:2609.08690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models expand model capacity without a proportional increase in training compute, but increasing sparsity makes reliable hyperparameter transfer challenging. In this work, we show that conventional hyperparameter scaling laws are insufficient for ultra-sparse MoEs: the optimal learning rate and batch size vary with activation ratio, and these shifts cannot be explained by either total or activated parameter count alone. To characterize this dependence, we conduct 1,800 pre-training runs spanning six activated-parameter scales and models with up to 6B total non-embedding parameters, processing approximately 20 trillion tokens at a cost of 200,000 equivalent H800 GPU-hours. Our results reconcile conflicting findings in prior work by revealing two scaling regimes. At fixed sparsity, the optimal batch size follows a power-law relationship with training tokens $D$, whereas the optimal learning rate scales with training compute $C$ and remains robust to the allocation between model size and data. Across sparsity levels, the activation ratio $A$ enters both relationships as an additional multiplicative power-law factor. These observations lead to unified hyperparameter scaling laws that transfer across MoE sparsity levels. Large-scale evaluation shows that the scaling form outperforms alternative functional forms. On a held-out ultra-sparse MoE with 12B total parameters and only 1/64 of its experts activated, the predicted hyperparameters remain close to the observed optima, supporting joint extrapolation across model scale and sparsity. Further experiments demonstrate transfer across expert granularities and isolate the effect of activation ratio from that of total expert count.

items.title: Answer-Distribution Trajectories: A Stochastic-Dynamics View of LLM Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Answer-Distribution Trajectories: A Stochastic-Dynamics View of LLM Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2609.09030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning provides a structured computation between a model's input and final answer. Yet it is often evaluated through endpoint accuracy, which ignores the path taken to reach that answer. An emerging line of work addresses this limitation using entropy profiles, which track how uncertainty evolves over the reasoning process but do not reveal which competing hypotheses account for that uncertainty. We introduce answer-distribution trajectories, a stochastic-dynamics-inspired representation that tracks the model's full predictive distribution over answers as reasoning unfolds. As a strictly finer representation than endpoint and entropy summaries, answer-distribution trajectories enable us to characterize a trace through a dynamical reasoning profile spanning exploration, revision, motion, and commitment, and to distinguish different dynamical mechanisms of reasoning success and failure. Across sixteen open-weight language models and four reasoning benchmarks, we show that traces with the same endpoint and similar entropy profiles can exhibit substantially different reasoning dynamics. We further find substantial variation in these dynamics both within and across models and tasks, with different objectives favoring different dynamical profiles. Additionally, we show that training and inference choices systematically reshape these profiles. Our results suggest that answer-distribution trajectories provide a rich framework for analysing and evaluating the dynamics of LLM reasoning.

items.title: SAEScientist-Bench: Can AI Agents Conduct Autonomous SAE Interpretability Research? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SAEScientist-Bench: Can AI Agents Conduct Autonomous SAE Interpretability Research?
items.summary: arXiv:2609.09113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While research on recursive self-improvement (RSI) has predominantly automated model training pipelines, reliable autonomous development demands a missing pillar: post-hoc monitoring and auditing to understand what models learn and ensure safe alignment. Mechanistic interpretability tools are essential to bridge this gap, among which Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) serve as a cornerstone by isolating interpretable features for model inspection and steering. In this paper, we introduce SAEScientist-Bench to evaluate whether AI agents can act as scientists utilizing SAE tools for autonomous mechanistic discovery. Given a target concept, an agent designs contrastive probes and navigates a Gemma Scope dictionary of 131K+ features in Gemma-2-9B-IT to discover the optimal feature, evaluated against curated expert reference features anchored on Neuronpedia across activation rank, concept selectivity on contrastive texts, and causal steering. Across 10 agent configurations and 20 tasks, frontier agents demonstrate genuine discovery capabilities and lead different evaluation dimensions, but remain well behind the expert baseline, approaching expert levels on separating target concepts from contrastive controls while lagging substantially in causal generation steering. Further analysis reveals that although agents can design contrasts to rule out spurious candidates, they frequently misinterpret experimental measurements. These results establish experimental model understanding as a measurable capability for closed-loop autonomous AI R&D. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trae1ounG/SAEScientist.

items.title: Introducing HALC: A general pipeline for the systematic and reliable construction of prompts for automated coding with LLMs in the computational social sciences [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Introducing HALC: A general pipeline for the systematic and reliable construction of prompts for automated coding with LLMs in the computational social sciences
items.summary: arXiv:2507.21831v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLMs are seeing widespread use for task automation, including automated coding in the social sciences. However, even though researchers have proposed different prompting strategies, their effectiveness varies across LLMs and tasks. Often trial and error practices are still widespread. Our study aims to fill this gap and evaluate how LLMs can be used in a systematic and transparent way to produce reliable codings in content analyses. We propose HALC-a general pipeline that allows for the systematic and reliable construction of prompts for any given coding task and model. We develop this pipeline based on current literature and findings of a prestudy investigating consistency and influencing factors of LLM codings. We also apply HALC on two other datasets covering different thematic contexts, document types, languages, and coding units to test its applicability. Based on more than three million LLM requests, our results demonstrate that the pipeline is capable of identifying prompts for reliable codings in different settings. We also discuss shortcomings and further potential for development.

items.title: Patent Representation Learning via Self-supervision [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Patent Representation Learning via Self-supervision
items.summary: arXiv:2511.10657v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study self-supervised patent representation learning with contrastive objectives. A standard baseline constructs positives by encoding the same text twice under independent dropout masks, but applying this recipe to long, structured patent documents requires careful calibration. We show that dropout-only training can be substantially strengthened by tuning temperature and dropout rate, yet its best configuration is evaluation-dependent and does not transfer uniformly from title--abstract retrieval to claim-to-disclosure retrieval. We propose mixed dropout--section positives, a patent-specific view construction strategy in which each positive pair links the title--abstract view of a patent either to a dropout re-encoding of itself or to another section of the same patent, such as claims, summary, background, drawings, or description. This uses patent-internal structure as a training-time signal without IPC labels, citations, or relevance annotations. We evaluate on graded EPO search-report retrieval, DAPFAM, a recently proposed family-level patent retrieval benchmark, and IPC subclass classification. Section-based positives improve over calibrated dropout-only and generic title--abstract augmentation baselines, are competitive with citation-informed patent encoders and a general-purpose embedding model, and perform strongly on the out-of-domain split of DAPFAM. Additional cross-section alignment diagnostics show that section-pair training improves compatibility among abstracts, claims, and descriptions of the same invention. These results indicate that patent sections provide effective self-supervised positive views for learning dense patent representations.

items.title: KDFlow: A User-Friendly and Efficient Knowledge Distillation Framework for Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: KDFlow: A User-Friendly and Efficient Knowledge Distillation Framework for Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2603.01875v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used to compress and post-train large language models (LLMs), yet many existing frameworks execute teacher inference with the same training-oriented backend as student optimization, leading to suboptimal efficiency. In this paper, we propose KDFlow, a novel framework for LLM distillation that features a decoupled architecture and employs SGLang for teacher inference. KDFlow combines SGLang for teacher inference with PyTorch FSDP2 for student optimization, allowing each model to run on a backend tailored to its workload. To enable efficient full-vocabulary distillation in this decoupled architecture, KDFlow transfers the teacher's final hidden states via Ray's object store and recomputes teacher logits on each student worker using a frozen copy of the teacher's output head. Furthermore, our framework supports both off-policy and on-policy distillation and incorporates cross-tokenizer algorithms through highly extensible and user-friendly APIs. Experiments show that KDFlow achieves a 1.44$\times$ to 6.36$\times$ speedup over MS-SWIFT in off-policy distillation and a 1.43$\times$ to 1.75$\times$ speedup over verl in on-policy distillation. KDFlow further scales to 64 GPUs, achieving 3.68$\times$ and 2.52$\times$ strong-scaling speedups in two representative model configurations. The code and documentation are publicly available.

items.title: AdaExplore: Failure-Driven Adaptation and Diversity-Preserving Search for Efficient Kernel Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AdaExplore: Failure-Driven Adaptation and Diversity-Preserving Search for Efficient Kernel Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2604.16625v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent large language model (LLM) agents have shown promise in using execution feedback for test-time adaptation. However, robust self-improvement remains far from solved: most approaches still treat each problem instance independently, without accumulating reusable knowledge. This limitation is particularly pronounced in domain-specific languages such as Triton, which are underrepresented in LLM pretraining data. Their strict constraints and non-linear optimization landscape further make naive generation and local refinement unreliable. We propose AdaExplore, an agent framework that enables self-improvement via accumulated execution feedback for performance-critical kernel code generation through two complementary stages: failure-driven adaptation and diversity-preserving search, jointly improving correctness and optimization performance without additional fine-tuning or external knowledge. In the adaptation stage, the agent synthesizes tasks and converts recurring failures into a reusable memory of validity rules, helping subsequent generations remain within the feasible set. In the search stage, the agent organizes candidate kernels as a tree and alternates between small local refinements and larger structural regeneration, allowing it to explore the optimization landscape beyond local optima. Experiments on kernel runtime optimization benchmarks validate these gains: AdaExplore achieves 3.11x and 1.62x speedups on KernelBench Level-2 and Level-3, respectively, within 100 steps, and continues to improve with additional computation.

items.title: FragileFlow: Spectral Control of Correct-but-Fragile Predictions for Foundation Model Robustness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FragileFlow: Spectral Control of Correct-but-Fragile Predictions for Foundation Model Robustness
items.summary: arXiv:2605.08896v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robust adaptation of LLMs and VLMs is often evaluated by average accuracy or average consistency under perturbations. However, these averages can hide a structured failure mode: a prediction may remain correct while probability mass already flows from particular true classes toward systematic wrong competitors near the decision boundary. In this paper, we formalize this phenomenon as margin-aware error flow and introduce FragileFlow, a plug-in regularizer that uses a calibrated margin buffer to identify correct-but-fragile predictions and organize their off-class probability mass into a class-wise vulnerable-risk matrix. Theoretically, we provide the first PAC-Bayes upper bound for this margin-aware error-flow object, showing how empirical spectral control yields a conservative route to deterministic worst-class robustness under a stability condition. Experiments on multiple-choice LLM benchmarks and few-shot CLIP adaptation show that FragileFlow consistently improves the proposed theory-facing risk measures over matched baselines, yields perturbed worst-class accuracy gains in most settings, and preserves clean accuracy across comparisons.

items.title: Generating Pretraining Tokens from Organic Data for Data-Bound Scaling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Generating Pretraining Tokens from Organic Data for Data-Bound Scaling
items.summary: arXiv:2605.17849v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM pretraining is shifting from a compute-bound to a data-bound regime, where available human (organic) text falls far short of scaling demands. However, reaching the data-bound regime does not mean the model has fully utilized its organic corpus. In this paper, we introduce SynPro, a synthetic data generation framework that helps LLMs more thoroughly learn from limited organic data. SynPro applies two operations, rephrasing and reformatting, that present the same organic source in diverse forms to facilitate deeper learning without introducing external information. Both generators are optimized via reinforcement learning with quality, faithfulness, and data influence rewards, and are continuously updated as pretraining plateaus to target content the model has yet to absorb. We pretrain 400M, 1.1B, and 2B models with 10% of their Chinchilla-optimal tokens (0.8B, 2.2B, and 4B) from DCLM-Baseline, reflecting a realistic data-bound regime in frontier pretraining. Our results reveal that organic data is significantly underutilized by standard repetition: SynPro unlocks 3.4--5.2x the effective tokens of repetition, even surpassing the non-data-bound oracle that trains on equivalent unique data at the 1.1B and 2B scales. Analyses confirm that faithful, model-aware synthesis sustains data-bound scaling without causing distribution collapse. We open-source our code at https://github.com/cxcscmu/SynPro.

items.title: More Context, Larger Models, or Moral Knowledge? A Systematic Study of Schwartz Value Detection in Political Texts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: More Context, Larger Models, or Moral Knowledge? A Systematic Study of Schwartz Value Detection in Political Texts
items.summary: arXiv:2605.22641v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Detecting Schwartz values in political texts is hard: cues are often implicit, and neighboring values differ by fine distinctions. Two remedies are widely assumed to help: more surrounding document text, and explicit moral knowledge. Knowledge-based retrieval has improved benchmarks elsewhere, but whether either transfers here is untested, because published systems vary context, knowledge, and model family at once. We separate these factors under matched conditions on the ValuesML/Touch\'e ValueEval format. The input ranges from the target sentence to a local window to the full document. Retrieval is either absent or drawn from a curated moral knowledge base, injected by early, late, or cross-attention fusion. Supervised DeBERTa-v3 encoders are compared against zero-shot LLMs from 12B to 123B. More context is not uniformly better: full-document input improves the encoders by 2.5-3.8 macro-F1 points but does not consistently help the LLMs. Retrieved knowledge helps more reliably, improving every model family and context under early fusion. A control substituting random knowledge-base entries shows the families gain differently: LLMs from relevance, encoders from exposure to the value ontology. Neither larger encoders nor larger LLMs guarantee gains, and early fusion outperforms both trainable variants. Value-sensitive NLP should evaluate context, knowledge, and model family jointly.

items.title: Clarify, Abstain or Answer? Strategising in Conversation with Belief-Augmented Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Clarify, Abstain or Answer? Strategising in Conversation with Belief-Augmented Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2605.25831v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) define a distribution over text, which can be viewed as a probabilistic representation of uncertainty: sampling K responses yields a belief state - responses a model deems plausible. Existing work exploits this representation for narrow tasks like either decoding or selective prediction, and often requires manual interventions, not controlling generation directly. We propose Belief-Augmented Generation (BAG): grounding LLMs in their own belief state via the prompt and letting them reason over these K samples to decide on and execute a conversational strategy: clarify, abstain, or answer. In a multi-turn ambiguous question answering (QA) setting, we find that LLMs by default rarely clarify or abstain, ignoring uncertainty about the input (aleatoric) or facts (epistemic). BAG improves QA accuracy across six models and yields strategy decisions more faithful to their belief state than prompt-only baselines. Disentangling when to clarify from when to abstain, however, remains challenging.

items.title: LayerRoute: Input-Conditioned Adaptive Layer Skipping via LoRA Fine-Tuning for Agentic Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LayerRoute: Input-Conditioned Adaptive Layer Skipping via LoRA Fine-Tuning for Agentic Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2606.01838v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic language model systems alternate between two structurally distinct step types: structured tool calls (short, deterministic, low perplexity) and open-ended planning/reasoning steps (long, complex, high perplexity). Despite this heterogeneity, current inference systems apply identical compute to every step. We introduce LayerRoute, a lightweight adapter that learns to selectively skip transformer blocks on a per-input basis. LayerRoute augments each of the 24 transformer blocks in Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with: (1) a per-layer router (~897 parameters, Linear(896,1)) that outputs a hard binary gate via the straight-through estimator, and (2) LoRA adapters (rank 8, ~1.08M parameters) on the Q/K/V/O attention projections. The backbone weights remain frozen. A single end-to-end training pass on agentic data (Hermes, Glaive, GSM8K, Turing) with a gate regularisation term forces the system to discover which blocks are skippable per input type. After 3,000 steps (6.4 minutes on an A100 40GB), LayerRoute achieves a 12.91% skip differential: tool calls skip 15.25% of FLOPs while planning steps skip only 2.34%, using only 1.10M trainable parameters (0.22% of the 494M backbone). Quality improves over the base model due to LoRA adaptation, with perplexity delta of -1.29 on tool calls and -1.30 on planning.

items.title: When New Generators Arrive: Lifelong Machine-Generated Text Attribution via Ridge Feature Transfer [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When New Generators Arrive: Lifelong Machine-Generated Text Attribution via Ridge Feature Transfer
items.summary: arXiv:2606.05626v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine-generated text (MGT) attribution aims to identify the specific generator responsible for a given text, thereby providing fine-grained evidence for model accountability and misuse investigation. As new large language models continue to emerge, attribution models must continuously incorporate new generators while preserving their ability to recognize previously seen ones. Prior works have shown that this lifelong MGT attribution setting is challenging, and existing methods often struggle to achieve a stable balance between adapting to new classes and retaining old ones. To address this issue, we propose RidgeFT, a lightweight analytic update framework that does not rely on exemplar replay. RidgeFT trains a task-aware encoder on the initial generator set, stores compact class-wise sufficient statistics when each generator class is first observed, and then freezes the encoder for replay-free closed-form updates. It then suppresses generator-irrelevant variation through covariance calibration, improves representation capacity with fixed random features, and updates new classes through closed-form ridge regression based on class-level sufficient statistics. Across multi-topic evaluations with varying initial generator setups, RidgeFT consistently outperforms baselines. It achieves the best overall macro-F1 across domains, backbones, and incremental protocols, while also improving both old-class retention and new-class adaptation. These results suggest that feature-stable analytic updates provide a simple yet effective approach to lifelong MGT attribution.
